title: I. At Grushenka’s
paragraphs: Alyosha made his way to the cathedral square, to the widow Morozov's house, to see Grushenka, who had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message begging him to come. Questioning Fenya, Alyosha learned that her mistress had been particularly distressed since the day before. In the two months that had passed since Mitya's arrest, Alyosha had called frequently at the widow Morozov's house, both from his own inclination and to bring messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya's arrest, Grushenka had fallen very ill, and had been ill for nearly five weeks. For one whole week she had been unconscious. She was much changed — thinner and a little sallow — though she had been well enough to go out for the past fortnight. But to Alyosha her face was even more attractive than before, and he liked to meet her eyes when he went in to her. A look of firmness and intelligent purpose had developed in her face. There were signs of a spiritual transformation in her, and a steadfast, fine, humble resolve that nothing could shake could be seen in her. There was a small vertical line between her brows that gave her charming face a look of concentrated thought, almost austere at first glance. There was scarcely a trace left of her former frivolity.

It seemed strange to Alyosha, too, that in spite of the calamity that had overtaken the poor girl — betrothed to a man arrested for a terrible crime almost at the moment of their betrothal — in spite of her illness and the almost inevitable sentence hanging over Mitya, Grushenka had not yet lost her youthful cheerfulness. There was a soft light in the once proud eyes, though at times they flashed with the old vindictive fire when she was visited by one disturbing thought that had grown stronger than ever in her heart. The object of that uneasiness was still the same — Katerina Ivanovna, about whom Grushenka had even raved while lying delirious. Alyosha knew she was fearfully jealous of her. Yet Katerina Ivanovna had not once visited Mitya in prison, though she might have done so any time she liked. All this created a difficult problem for Alyosha, for he was the only person to whom Grushenka opened her heart, and from whom she was constantly asking advice. Sometimes he was unable to say anything.

Full of anxiety he entered her lodging. She was at home. She had come back from seeing Mitya half an hour earlier, and from the quick movement with which she sprang up from her chair to meet him he could see she had been expecting him with great impatience. A pack of cards dealt for a game of “fools” lay on the table. A bed had been made up on the leather sofa across from it, and Maximov lay on it, half-reclining. He was wearing a dressing gown and a cotton nightcap, and was clearly ill and weak, though he was smiling blissfully. When the homeless old man had come back with Grushenka from Mokroe two months before, he had simply stayed on, and was still staying with her. He had arrived with her in rain and sleet, sat down on the sofa, drenched and scared, and gazed at her mutely with a timid, pleading smile. Grushenka, who was in terrible grief and in the first stage of fever, had almost forgotten his existence amid everything she had to do in the first half-hour after arriving. Then she happened to look at him closely: he gave a pitiful, helpless little laugh. She called Fenya and told her to bring him something to eat. All that day he sat in the same place, almost without stirring. When it got dark and the shutters were closed, Fenya asked her mistress:
“Is the gentleman going to stay the night, mistress?”
“Yes — make him a bed on the sofa,” Grushenka answered.

Questioning him more carefully, Grushenka learned from him that he literally had nowhere to go, and that “Mr. Kalganov, my benefactor, told me straight out that he wouldn't receive me again, and gave me five roubles.”

“Well, God bless you, you'd better stay, then,” Grushenka decided in her grief, smiling at him compassionately. Her smile wrung the old man's heart, and his lips twitched with grateful tears. And so the destitute wanderer had stayed with her ever since. He did not leave the house even while she was ill. Fenya and her grandmother the cook did not turn him out, but went on serving him meals and making up his bed on the sofa. Grushenka had grown used to him, and coming back from seeing Mitya (whom she had started visiting in prison before she was really well) she would sit down and start chatting with “Maximushka” about trivial matters, to keep herself from dwelling on her sorrow. The old man turned out to be a good storyteller on occasion, so that in the end she found him a necessity. Apart from Alyosha — who didn't come every day and never stayed long — Grushenka saw scarcely anyone. Her old merchant lay gravely ill at this time, “at his last gasp,” as they said around town, and he did indeed die a week after Mitya's trial. Three weeks before his death, sensing the end drawing near, he had at last summoned his sons, their wives, and their children upstairs and told them not to leave him again. From that moment he gave strict orders to his servants not to admit Grushenka, and to tell her, if she came, “The master wishes you long life and happiness, and tells you to forget him.” But Grushenka sent almost every day to ask after him.

“You've come at last!” she cried, tossing aside the cards and greeting Alyosha joyfully. “Maximushka has been scaring me that perhaps you wouldn't come. Ah, how I need you! Sit down at the table. What will you have — coffee?”
“Yes, please,” Alyosha said, sitting down at the table. “I'm very hungry.”

“That's good. Fenya, Fenya, coffee,” Grushenka cried. “It's been ready for you for ages. And bring some little pies, and mind they're hot. Do you know, we've had a storm over those pies today. I took them to the prison for him, and would you believe, he threw them back at me: he wouldn't eat them. He flung one of them on the floor and stamped on it. So I said to him, ‘I'll leave them with the warder; if you don't eat them by evening, then your venomous spite is enough to feed you!' With that, I left. We had another quarrel, would you believe it? Every time I go, we quarrel.”
Grushenka said all this in one breath in her agitation. Maximov, feeling nervous, smiled at once and stared at the floor.
“What did you quarrel about this time?” Alyosha asked.

“I didn't expect it in the least. Just imagine — he's jealous of the Pole. ‘Why are you keeping him?' he said. ‘So you've started keeping him.' He's jealous, jealous of me all the time — jealous over my eating and sleeping! Last week he even took it into his head to be jealous of Kuzma.”
“But he knew about the Pole before?”

“Yes, exactly. He has known about him from the very beginning, but today he suddenly got going and began scolding me about him. I'm ashamed to repeat what he said. Silly fool! Rakitin went in as I was leaving. Maybe Rakitin is egging him on. What do you think?” she added carelessly.
“He loves you — that's what it is. He loves you so much. And right now he's especially worried.”

“I should think so, with the trial tomorrow. I went to him to say something about tomorrow, because I dread to think what's going to happen then. You say he's worried — but how worried am I! And he talks about the Pole! He's too silly! At least he's not jealous of Maximushka yet.”
“My wife was dreadfully jealous over me too,” Maximov put in.
“Jealous of you?” Grushenka laughed in spite of herself. “Of whom could she have been jealous?”
“Of the servant girls.”

“Hush, Maximushka, I'm in no mood for laughing now; I'm angry. Don't stare at the pies. I won't give you any — they're no good for you, and I won't give you any vodka either. I have to look after him, too, as though I ran an almshouse,” she laughed.
“I don't deserve your kindness. I'm a worthless creature,” said Maximov, with tears in his voice. “You'd do better spending your kindness on people more useful than me.”

“Ech, everyone has some use, Maximushka — how can anyone say who's the most useful? If only that Pole didn't exist, Alyosha. He's taken it into his head to fall ill today too. I went to see him as well. And I'll send him some pies — on purpose. I hadn't been sending him any, but Mitya accused me of it, so now I'll send some! Ah, here's Fenya with a letter! Yes, it's from the Poles — begging again!”

Pan Mussyalovitch had in fact sent an extremely long and, in his characteristic fashion, eloquent letter, begging her to lend him three roubles. Enclosed with the letter was a receipt for the sum, with a promise to repay it within three months, signed by Pan Vrublevsky as well. Grushenka had received many such letters, accompanied by such receipts, from her former lover during the fortnight of her convalescence. But she knew the two Poles had come to ask after her health during her illness. The first letter Grushenka got from them was a long one, written on large notepaper with a big family crest on the seal. It was so obscure and rhetorical that Grushenka put it down before she'd read half of it, unable to make head or tail of it. She couldn't be bothered with letters then. The first letter was followed next day by another, in which Pan Mussyalovitch begged her for a loan of two thousand roubles for a very short period. Grushenka left that letter unanswered too. A whole series of letters followed — one a day — all as pompous and rhetorical, but the sum asked for gradually shrank, down to a hundred roubles, then to twenty-five, to ten, and finally Grushenka received a letter in which both Poles begged her for a single rouble, enclosing a receipt signed by both.

At that point Grushenka suddenly felt sorry for them, and at dusk she went over to their lodging herself. She found the two Poles in great poverty, almost destitute, without food or fuel, without cigarettes, in debt to their landlady. The two hundred roubles they had carried off from Mitya at Mokroe had soon disappeared. But Grushenka was surprised to find them receiving her with arrogant dignity and self-assertion, with the greatest punctilio and pompous speeches. Grushenka simply laughed, and gave her former admirer ten roubles. Then, laughing, she told Mitya about it, and he was not in the least jealous. But ever since, the Poles had attached themselves to Grushenka and bombarded her daily with requests for money, and she had always sent them small sums. And now, that day, Mitya had taken it into his head to be fearfully jealous.

“Like a fool, I went round to him just for a minute on the way to see Mitya, because he's ill too, my Pole,” Grushenka began again in nervous haste. “I was laughing, telling Mitya about it. ‘Imagine,' I said, ‘my Pole had the happy idea of singing his old songs to me on the guitar. He thought I'd be touched and marry him!' Mitya leapt up swearing. So, there — I'll send them the pies! Fenya, is that the little girl they've sent? Here, give her three roubles, and pack up a dozen pies in paper for her and tell her to take them. And you, Alyosha, be sure to tell Mitya that I did send them the pies.”
“I wouldn't tell him for anything,” Alyosha said, smiling.
“Ech, you think he's unhappy about it. Why, he's jealous on purpose. He doesn't care,” Grushenka said bitterly.
“On purpose?” Alyosha asked.

“I'm telling you, you're silly, Alyosha. You know nothing about it, for all your cleverness. I'm not offended that he's jealous of a girl like me. I'd be offended if he weren't jealous. That's who I am. I'm not offended by jealousy. I have a fierce heart too. I can be jealous myself. What offends me is that he doesn't love me at all. I'm telling you he's jealous now _on purpose_. Am I blind? Don't I see? Just now he started talking to me about that woman, about Katerina — saying she's this and that, how she has ordered a doctor from Moscow for him, to try to save him, and hired the best legal counsel, the most learned one too. So he loves her, if he'll praise her to my face — all the more shame to him! He's treated me badly himself, so he's turned on me, to make out that I'm the one at fault first, and shift it all onto me. ‘You were with your Pole before me, so I can't be blamed for Katerina,' — that's what it amounts to. He wants to pin the whole blame on me. He went at me on purpose, on purpose, I tell you, but I'll —”
Grushenka couldn't finish saying what she would do. She hid her eyes in her handkerchief and sobbed violently.
“He doesn't love Katerina Ivanovna,” Alyosha said firmly.

“Well, whether he loves her or not, I'll soon find out for myself,” Grushenka said, with a menacing note in her voice, taking the handkerchief from her eyes. Her face was distorted. Alyosha saw sadly that from being mild and serene, it had become sullen and spiteful.

“Enough of this foolishness,” she said suddenly. “That's not why I sent for you. Alyosha, darling — tomorrow — what will happen tomorrow? That's what's eating at me! And I'm the only one it's eating at! I look at everyone, and no one is thinking about it. No one cares. Are you even thinking about it? Tomorrow they'll try him, you know. Tell me, how will he be tried? It was the valet — the valet killed him! Good heavens! Can they convict him in place of the valet, and will no one stand up for him? They haven't bothered the valet at all, have they?”

“He's been severely cross-examined,” Alyosha observed thoughtfully, “but everyone came to the conclusion it wasn't him. Now he's lying very ill. He's been ill ever since that attack. Really ill,” Alyosha added.
“Oh, dear! Couldn't you go to that counsel yourself and tell him the whole thing in person? They say he's been brought from Petersburg for three thousand roubles.”

“We put up the three thousand together — Ivan, Katerina Ivanovna, and I — but she paid two thousand for the doctor from Moscow herself. The counsel, Fetyukovitch, would have charged more, but the case has become known all over Russia; it's being talked of in every newspaper and journal. Fetyukovitch agreed to come more for the glory of the thing, because the case has become so notorious. I saw him yesterday.”
“Well? Did you talk to him?” Grushenka put in eagerly.
“He listened and said nothing. He told me he's already formed his opinion. But he promised to give my words consideration.”
“Consideration! Ah, they're swindlers! They'll ruin him. And why did she send for the doctor?”
“As an expert. They want to prove Mitya's mad, and that he committed the murder when he didn't know what he was doing.” Alyosha smiled gently. “But Mitya won't agree to that.”

“Yes — and that would be the truth if he had killed him!” Grushenka cried. “He was mad then, perfectly mad, and it was my fault, wretch that I am! But of course he didn't do it, he didn't do it! And they're all against him, the whole town. Even Fenya's testimony went to prove he did it. And the people at the shop, and that official, and at the tavern too — before, people had heard him say so! They are all, all against him, all crying out against him.”
“Yes, there's a fearful accumulation of evidence,” Alyosha observed grimly.
“And Grigory — Grigory Vassilyevitch — sticks to his story that the door was open, insists he saw it — there's no shaking him. I went and talked to him myself. He's rude about it too.”
“Yes, that's perhaps the strongest evidence against him,” Alyosha said.

“And as for Mitya being mad, he certainly seems like it now,” Grushenka began with a peculiarly anxious and mysterious air. “Do you know, Alyosha, I've been wanting to talk to you about this for a long time. I go to him every day and simply wonder at him. Tell me, now — what do you suppose he's always talking about? He talks and talks, and I can't make anything of it. I imagined he was talking about something intellectual that I was too foolish to understand. Then he suddenly started talking to me about a babe — about some child. ‘Why is the babe poor?' he said. ‘It's for that babe that I'm going to Siberia now. I am not a murderer, but I must go to Siberia!' What that meant, what babe, I couldn't tell for the life of me. Only I cried when he said it, because he said it so sweetly. He cried himself, and I cried too. He suddenly kissed me and made the sign of the cross over me. What did it mean, Alyosha, tell me? What is this babe?”
“It must be Rakitin, who's been going to see him lately,” Alyosha said, smiling, “though ... that's not Rakitin's doing. I didn't see Mitya yesterday. I'll see him today.”
“No, it's not Rakitin — it's his brother Ivan Fyodorovitch upsetting him. It's his visits — that's what it is,” Grushenka began, and suddenly broke off. Alyosha stared at her in amazement.
“Ivan's visits? Has he been to see him? Mitya told me himself that Ivan hasn't been once.”

“There ... there! What a girl I am! Blurting it out!” Grushenka exclaimed, confused, and suddenly blushing. “Wait, Alyosha, hush! Since I've said this much, I'll tell you the whole truth — he's been to see him twice, the first time right after he arrived. He galloped here from Moscow at once, of course, before I was taken ill; and the second time was a week ago. He told Mitya not to tell you about it under any circumstances — not to tell anyone, in fact. He came secretly.”
Alyosha sat plunged in thought, considering something. The news clearly struck him.

“Ivan doesn't talk to me about Mitya's case,” he said slowly. “He's said very little to me these last two months. And whenever I go to see him, he seems vexed that I've come, so I haven't been to see him for the last three weeks. Hm ... if he was there a week ago ... there certainly has been a change in Mitya this week.”

“There has been a change,” Grushenka agreed quickly. “They have a secret, they have a secret! Mitya told me himself there was a secret, and such a secret that Mitya can't rest. Before this he was cheerful — and indeed he is cheerful now — but when he shakes his head like that, you know, and strides around the room and keeps tugging at the hair on his right temple with his right hand, I know there's something weighing on his mind. I know! He was cheerful before — and indeed, he is cheerful today.”
“But you said he was worried.”

“Yes, he's worried, and yet cheerful. He keeps being irritable for a minute, then cheerful, then irritable again. And you know, Alyosha, I'm constantly amazed at him — with this awful thing hanging over him, he sometimes laughs at such trifles, as though he were a child himself.”
“And did he really tell you not to tell me about Ivan? Did he say, ‘Don't tell him'?”

“Yes, he said, ‘Don't tell him.' It's you Mitya's most afraid of. Because it's a secret — he said himself it was a secret. Alyosha, darling, go to him and find out what their secret is, and come and tell me,” Grushenka begged him with sudden eagerness. “Set my mind at rest so I know the worst that's in store for me. That's why I sent for you.”
“You think it's something to do with you? If it were, he wouldn't have told you there was a secret.”
“I don't know. Perhaps he wants to tell me, but doesn't dare. He's warning me. There is a secret, he tells me — but he won't tell me what it is.”
“What do you think yourself?”

“What do I think? It's the end for me, that's what I think. The three of them have been plotting my end — because Katerina's in it. It's all Katerina, it all comes from her. She's this and that — meaning that I'm not. He's telling me that in advance — warning me. He's planning to throw me over, that's the whole secret. They've planned it together, the three of them — Mitya, Katerina, and Ivan Fyodorovitch. Alyosha, I've been wanting to ask you for a long time. A week ago he suddenly told me that Ivan was in love with Katerina, because he often goes to see her. Did he tell me the truth, or not? Tell me on your conscience — tell me the worst.”
“I won't tell you a lie. Ivan is not in love with Katerina Ivanovna — I think.”

“Oh, that's what I thought! He's lying to me, shameless deceiver, that's what it is! And he was jealous of me just now, so he could throw the blame on me afterwards. He's stupid — he can't disguise what he's up to; he's so transparent, you know. But I'll give it to him, I'll give it to him! ‘You believe I did it,' he said. He said that to me, to me. He reproached me with that! God forgive him! You wait, I'll make it hot for Katerina at the trial! I'll just say one word then ... I'll tell everything then!”
And again she cried bitterly.

“This much I can tell you for certain, Grushenka,” Alyosha said, getting up. “First, that he loves you — loves you more than anyone in the world, and you alone. Believe me. I know. I do know. The second thing is that I don't want to worm his secret out of him, but if he tells me of his own accord today, I'll tell him straight out that I've promised to tell you. Then I'll come to you today and tell you. Only ... I have a feeling ... Katerina Ivanovna has nothing to do with it, and the secret is about something else. I'm sure of it. It hardly seems likely to be about Katerina Ivanovna — at least, that's how it seems to me. Good-bye for now.”

Alyosha shook her hand. Grushenka was still crying. He could see she put little faith in his consolation, but she was better for having cried herself out, for having spoken of it. He was sorry to leave her in such a state of mind, but he was in a hurry. He had a great many things still to do.
